questions.title: What a checklist tool assesses
questions.question: The checklist tool can be used to assess:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An annual student survey is a separate, standalone data-collection instrument in its own right, not something a checklist (a real-time, item-by-item observation tool) is used to conduct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Attendance rate is a longitudinal administrative metric tracked by a separate record system over time, not something captured by a single-encounter checklist.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Graduation rate is an institution-level outcome measured across a student's entire programme, far removed from the scope of a point-of-encounter checklist.
explanations.D: Correct. A checklist records whether specific, predefined criteria were met during an observed encounter, which suits capturing a satisfaction rating at that point in time. This is the answer both this module's Zagazig-campus and Fakous-campus Final papers mark for the identical question, confirming it is not a source-specific quirk. Among the four options, satisfaction is the only one that is itself an item-level, in-the-moment judgment rather than a longitudinal administrative record.

questions.learning_objective: State that a checklist tool is used to assess student satisfaction, not attendance or graduation rate.

questions.title: Foundation of the physician-patient relationship
questions.question: A strong physician-patient relationship is built on:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Billing and financial arrangements are administrative consequences of a relationship that already exists; they do not themselves generate the trust the relationship depends on.
explanations.B: Correct. Trust and open communication are what allow a patient to disclose sensitive information and follow a physician's advice, and what allow a physician to make sound decisions on incomplete information volunteered honestly. This is the foundation the relationship's therapeutic value rests on, distinguishing it from the merely transactional or incidental elements offered as distractors. Every other option describes something that can exist alongside the relationship without being what sustains it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A physician's unshared personal opinions and views play no defined role in building patient trust, and asserting them inappropriately can actively damage the relationship.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Social connections between physician and patient are neither necessary nor sufficient for a strong clinical relationship, which must function even between strangers meeting for the first time.

questions.learning_objective: State that a strong physician-patient relationship is built on trust and communication, not financial obligations or personal opinions.

questions.title: Base of the accountability preconditions model
questions.question: In the model of the preconditions leading to accountability, the base of this model is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Authority (the sanctioned power to act) is a separate precondition from the capacity to actually carry a task out, and is not the model's base layer as tested here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Professionalism is a broader orientation that shapes how accountability is exercised, not the specific foundational precondition this model names as its base.
explanations.C: Correct. Ability is the base of the model because a person cannot be meaningfully held accountable for a task they lack the capacity to perform — every later precondition (authority, responsibility) presupposes that the underlying ability already exists. This ordering reflects a common structure in accountability frameworks, where capability must precede the assignment of responsibility for a task to be fair or meaningful. Placing ability first is what makes the rest of the model coherent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Responsibility (being assigned or accepting a task) itself presupposes the ability to carry it out, making ability the more fundamental, earlier precondition, not the model's base.

questions.learning_objective: State that ability is the base precondition in the model leading to accountability.

questions.title: Storming stage of team development
questions.question: Conflict between team members and some rebellion uprising against the assigned tasks occur in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Performing is the stage where the team functions smoothly and productively, the opposite of the friction this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Forming is the initial orientation stage, before roles and authority have been contested enough to produce real conflict.
explanations.C: Correct. Storming is the stage in the standard forming-storming-norming-performing-adjourning model defined by conflict between team members and resistance to assigned tasks, as members test roles, authority and the group's working norms. It is an expected, not pathological, stage every functioning team model predicts a team will pass through. The stem's own language — conflict and rebellion against assigned tasks — maps directly onto storming's defining feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Norming is the stage where the team settles on agreed working conventions after the earlier conflict has been resolved, not while it is still occurring.

questions.learning_objective: Identify storming as the team-development stage marked by conflict and resistance to assigned tasks.

questions.title: Justice and fair distribution of resources
questions.question: A bioethical principle requires fair distribution of healthcare resources:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Respect for cultural diversity is a distinct ethical value concerned with honouring differing beliefs and practices, not with how scarce resources are allocated.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Non-stigmatization concerns avoiding unfair labelling or discrimination against a patient group, a related but separate concern from resource distribution itself.
explanations.C: Correct. Justice is one of the four core bioethical principles (alongside autonomy, beneficence and non-maleficence) and specifically concerns the fair distribution of scarce resources. It is invoked whenever a scenario is about who gets access to something limited, which is exactly what this stem describes. The other three options are each real ethical values, but none of them specifically governs distribution/allocation questions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Human dignity is a foundational value underlying all ethical practice broadly, but it does not specifically name the distribution-of-resources principle this stem asks about.

questions.learning_objective: Identify justice as the bioethical principle requiring fair distribution of healthcare resources.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-105 > Professional Practice I > Bioethical principles

questions.title: Self-assessment and constructive feedback
questions.question: A medical student receives feedback from their peers on a recent group project, highlighting areas for improvement in teamwork and communication. This scenario best illustrates which component of professionalism?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Scientific knowledge concerns the factual/theoretical content a student has mastered, not the act of receiving and using feedback about performance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Clinical skills refers to the underlying competence being demonstrated, not the process of self-assessment and improvement the stem specifically emphasises.
explanations.C: Correct. Receiving peer feedback and using it to identify areas for improvement is a direct illustration of professionalism's self-assessment-and-constructive-feedback component. This component is specifically about how a learner engages with evaluation of their own performance, which is exactly what the stem describes. The scenario is not primarily about what was learned or done, but about how the student responds to being assessed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Time management concerns organising tasks and deadlines, unrelated to the peer-feedback process this stem describes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a peer-feedback scenario as illustrating professionalism's self-assessment and constructive-feedback component.

questions.title: Definition of compassion in professionalism
questions.question: Compassion in medical professionalism is best described as:

options.B: Showing empathy and care towards patients

explanations.A: Incorrect. Maintaining professional distance describes an appropriate boundary, not compassion itself — the two are not mutually exclusive, but distance alone does not define compassion.
explanations.B: Correct. Compassion is showing empathy and care towards patients, engaging with their experience of illness rather than treating the encounter as purely transactional or task-focused. This is the value that most directly captures what compassion means in a clinical context. Each distractor instead names something that can coexist with compassion but is not itself the definition of it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Focusing on administrative duties describes a task orientation unrelated to, and potentially in tension with, showing care towards a patient.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prioritizing clinical tasks over the patient's emotional experience is closer to the opposite of compassionate care than a description of it.

questions.learning_objective: State that compassion in medical professionalism means showing empathy and care towards patients.

questions.title: Purpose of early professionalism education
questions.question: Early education on professional standards is important for medical students to:

explanations.A: Correct. Early education on professional standards establishes expectations and norms before lapses occur, which is why it helps prevent later disciplinary action. Introducing professionalism training early in the curriculum, rather than only after a violation, is the preventive logic behind why medical schools teach it from Year 1. This is the one option that describes a genuine, positive purpose of the education.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Professionalism education aims to prepare students for appropriate patient contact, not to avoid it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Professionalism training actively discourages cheating and other integrity violations; it does not encourage them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no purpose or mechanism by which early professionalism education would delay graduation — if anything, it supports timely progression by reducing disciplinary interruptions.

questions.learning_objective: State that early professionalism education is important chiefly to prevent later disciplinary action.

questions.title: Emergency exception to informed consent
questions.question: The consent is not necessary in emergency cases for:

explanations.A: Correct. The emergency exception to informed consent is narrowly scoped to lifesaving operations, where the patient cannot consent and withholding treatment would cost life; the presumption is that a reasonable patient would want the care. This narrow scope is exactly what distinguishes the true emergency exception from a much broader (and incorrect) claim that any urgent-feeling situation dispenses with consent. It applies to genuinely life-or-death situations only.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Any medical procedure" over-generalises the exception far beyond its actual scope — consent is still required for the overwhelming majority of medical procedures, even urgent ones that are not life-threatening.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Non-life-threatening operations still require consent even under time pressure, since the emergency exception's justification (imminent death without treatment) does not apply.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cosmetic surgery is elective by definition and always requires consent; it is never the kind of situation the emergency exception was designed for.

questions.learning_objective: State that the emergency exception to informed consent applies specifically to lifesaving operations.

questions.title: Short-term-fix conflict-resolution strategy
questions.question: A conflict-resolution strategy which allows you to resolve a problem in the short-term while working toward a long-term solution:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Competing describes one side winning outright, an approach that resolves nothing collaboratively and is not oriented toward any long-term solution.
explanations.B: Incorrect textbook-wise, but this is the source's own printed key of "C" mapped to the third-listed option, Accommodating — note that the stem's own definition (short-term fix while working toward a longer-term solution) is the standard definition of compromising, not accommodating. This mismatch is flagged in the concept's own uncertainty field; the printed key stands as printed per LANE-CARD.md §7, but the module's teaching content documents the textbook-correct fact rather than silently reproducing the mismatch as if uncontested.
explanations.C: Correct as printed (source key). The page's own printed key line reads "10) C", indexing this position, labelled "Accommodating" in this paper's option list. Textbook conflict-resolution theory instead defines this short-term-fix-while-working-toward-a-long-term-solution description as compromising (a mutual, partial concession), not accommodating (fully yielding to the other party) — flagged for reviewer attention rather than silently resolved.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Avoiding means not engaging with the conflict at all, which resolves nothing, whether short- or long-term.

questions.learning_objective: State the textbook definition of compromising as a short-term fix pursued alongside a longer-term solution, and recognise this source's printed-key/textbook-definition mismatch.

questions.title: Why professionalism matters
questions.question: Maintaining professionalism is important for medical students and doctors to:

options.A: Create a competitive environment among colleagues
options.B: Challenge the authority of senior healthcare professionals
options.C: Support the trust the public has in doctors
options.D: Prioritize personal interests over patient care

explanations.A: Incorrect. Professionalism norms discourage inter-colleague competitiveness in favour of collaboration; fostering competition is not a purpose professionalism serves.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Professionalism does not exist to challenge senior authority — appropriate escalation of concerns is different from generalised challenge to authority as a professionalism goal.
explanations.C: Correct. Maintaining professionalism is important because it supports the trust the public places in doctors as a group — patients and society rely on the profession collectively upholding standards for that trust to be warranted. This public-trust rationale is professionalism's outward-facing purpose, distinguishing it from the internally-focused, and actively discouraged, behaviours in the other options. It is the answer that describes a genuine positive function of professionalism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prioritizing personal interests over patient care is precisely what professionalism norms are designed to prevent, not something professionalism serves.

questions.learning_objective: State that maintaining professionalism supports the public's trust in doctors.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-105 > Professional Practice I > Professional duties

questions.title: Best method for self-assessment
questions.question: The best method for self-assessment:

explanations.A: Correct. Reflective practice — deliberately reviewing one's own performance and reasoning after an event — is the best method for self-assessment because it is the learner's own structured self-reflection, matching the definition of self-assessment itself. Peer and external evaluation are valuable feedback sources, but they rely on someone else's judgment rather than the learner assessing their own performance. Reflective practice is the method that keeps the assessment genuinely self-directed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ignoring mistakes is not a method of assessment at all — it is the absence of assessment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peer evaluation is a valuable feedback source, but it is assessment by someone else, not self-assessment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. External evaluation, like peer evaluation, is judgment from outside the learner, not the learner's own self-assessment process.

questions.learning_objective: State that reflective practice is the best method for self-assessment.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-105 > Professional Practice I > Assessment and feedback tools

questions.title: Onset of the physician-patient relationship
questions.question: The relationship between the physician and the patient starts when the patient:

options.A: Goes to the physician for care.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Going for care is typically the first clinical encounter, a milestone that is close in time to, but conceptually distinct from, the relationship's formal onset.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Receiving a bill is an administrative consequence that occurs well after the relationship has already begun, not its starting point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Being diagnosed happens even later in the clinical process, after the relationship and the encounter that produced the diagnosis have both already started.
explanations.D: Correct. The physician-patient relationship is formally considered to begin at the point the patient selects the physician, since selection/acceptance is the moment both parties enter into the relationship, even before any clinical activity has occurred. This distinguishes the relationship's legal and ethical onset from its later clinical or administrative milestones. Selecting the physician is the earliest of the four options in the actual sequence of events.

questions.learning_objective: State that the physician-patient relationship begins when the patient selects the physician.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-105 > Professional Practice I > Physician-patient relationship

questions.title: Definition of vertical equity
questions.question: Working based on need and the fact that different social groups have different health needs and some of which require more health care than others is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Equality means identical treatment regardless of differing need, the opposite of the need-based differentiation this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Horizontal equity means equal treatment for people with equal need, a related but distinct principle from allocating differently across groups with different needs.
explanations.C: Correct. Vertical equity is the principle of allocating health resources according to differing need, recognising that different social groups require different amounts of healthcare and providing proportionally rather than identically. This is exactly the need-based differentiation the stem describes. It is distinguished from horizontal equity by operating across groups with unequal needs, not within a group of equal need.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Integrity is an unrelated professional value about honesty and consistency, not a resource-allocation principle.

questions.learning_objective: Define vertical equity as need-based differential care, distinguishing it from horizontal equity and equality.

questions.title: Justice in organ transplant allocation
questions.question: The medical ethic related to allocating limited organ transplants without discrimination based on race, gender, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, religion, or any other social category, is .......

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomy concerns respecting a patient's own informed choices, not how a scarce resource is allocated across a population.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beneficence concerns acting for a specific patient's benefit, not the fairness of a distribution rule applied across candidates.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Non-maleficence concerns avoiding harm to a patient, a different concern from allocation fairness.
explanations.D: Correct. Justice is the bioethical principle governing fair, non-discriminatory allocation of scarce resources such as organ transplants — exactly the allocation-without-discrimination scenario the stem describes. Among the four core bioethical principles, only justice specifically addresses distribution/allocation dilemmas of this kind. The other three each concern a different ethical dimension of care that does not match this stem.

questions.learning_objective: Identify justice as the bioethical principle behind non-discriminatory allocation of limited organ transplants.

questions.title: Consent proxy in mental incapacity
questions.question: In mental disease which of the following has the right to give permission on behalf of that patient:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Friends have no formal standing to consent on a patient's behalf regardless of the closeness of the relationship.
explanations.B: Correct as marked in this source. The highlighted key names the patient's own treating physician as holding the right to consent on the patient's behalf in mental disease, reflecting the physician's direct clinical relationship and duty of care. Note this is flagged for reviewer attention: many medical-ethics curricula instead expect a court-appointed or other legal authority as the proxy for an incapacitated patient's consent, so this fact is worth a department-book cross-check before publication rather than being treated as beyond question.
explanations.C: Not selected in this source (see the correct-answer explanation for why this option is worth a second look) — "legally authority" (a court-appointed guardian or similar legal proxy) is the answer many medical-ethics curricula would expect for incapacitated-patient consent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neighbors, like friends, have no formal standing to consent on a patient's behalf.

questions.learning_objective: State, with reviewer-flagged uncertainty, that this source names the patient's own physician as the consent proxy in mental incapacity.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-105 > Professional Practice I > Consent and capacity

questions.title: Negotiation as a leadership skill
questions.question: Regarding leadership skills, understanding the interests of all involved parties and working to reach a solution that satisfies each one is referred to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Conflict-resolution" is the broader category this specific skill belongs to, but the stem names a more specific process than the general category alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Communication is the means by which interests are exchanged, but the stem describes a goal-directed process of reaching a mutually satisfying solution, which is more specific than communication alone.
explanations.C: Correct. Negotiation is specifically the leadership skill of understanding all parties' interests and working toward a solution that satisfies each one. This goal-directed, multi-party-interest-satisfying process is precisely what negotiation names, distinguishing it from the broader category (conflict-resolution) and from the means (communication) that supports it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reliability is an unrelated personal trait about consistency and dependability, not a process for reconciling multiple parties' interests.

questions.learning_objective: Identify negotiation as the leadership skill of understanding all parties' interests and reaching a mutually satisfying solution.

questions.title: Remedy for a pattern of wrong decisions
questions.question: Mona is a medical student, she usually makes wrong decisions, does not have the ability to understand her motivations preferences, or personality. What does the need to do?

options.A: To spend more hours in studying her lessons
options.B: To increase her level of self-awareness
options.C: To stop having fun with her friends

explanations.A: Incorrect. Studying more hours addresses a knowledge gap, not the self-understanding gap the stem specifically describes.
explanations.B: Correct. A person who habitually makes wrong decisions because they cannot understand their own motivations, preferences or personality needs to increase their self-awareness — the deficit described is specifically about self-understanding, and self-awareness is the construct that names it. Increasing self-awareness addresses the actual gap, unlike the other options, which either misdiagnose the problem or avoid it entirely. This is why self-awareness, not general study effort, is the targeted remedy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Withdrawing from friends does not address a self-understanding deficit and has no established link to improving decision-making of this kind.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ignoring the problem addresses nothing and would leave the underlying pattern of wrong decisions unchanged.

questions.learning_objective: State that increasing self-awareness is the remedy for a pattern of wrong decisions rooted in not understanding one's own motivations.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-105 > Professional Practice I > Self-awareness and emotional intelligence

questions.title: Outcome of good self-awareness
questions.question: Good level of self-awareness leads to:

options.D: Setting appropriate life and career goals

questions.title: What affects self-awareness
questions.question: We can gain self-awareness from different sources, which of the following statements describes these sources correctly?

options.A: Negative situations don't help us to gain self-awareness
options.B: All people have the same level of self-awareness
options.C: Self-awareness is affected by behavior and perception
options.D: You cannot improve your level of self-awareness

explanations.A: Incorrect. Negative situations are, in fact, a real source people draw self-awareness from, contradicting this option's absolute claim.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Self-awareness varies considerably between individuals; it is not uniform across all people.
explanations.C: Correct. Self-awareness is affected by, and can be gained from, one's own behaviour and perception — both how a person acts and how they perceive themselves and situations shape their self-understanding. This is the correctly-hedged, affirmative statement among four options, three of which are false absolutes ("don't help", "same level", "cannot improve"). Note the source itself prints this option's letter as "E" in an A/B/E/C sequence, a labeling slip in the original exam rather than a fifth real option.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Self-awareness is described as buildable and improvable (for example, through self-analysis), directly contradicting this option's claim that it cannot be changed.

questions.learning_objective: State that self-awareness is affected by behaviour and perception, rejecting false-absolute distractors about it.

questions.title: Definition of time management
questions.question: Time management, means to:

options.A: Stop have fun and work all of the day
options.B: Spend the time available to you much more effectively
options.C: Do everything for yourselves and never delegate

explanations.A: Incorrect. Eliminating all leisure to work constantly is not what time management means, and is not an effective or sustainable strategy.
explanations.B: Correct. Time management means spending the time available to you much more effectively — using time well, which can include delegating tasks and preserving rest, not maximising hours worked. This is the correctly-hedged definition among four options that each describe a common misconception about time management. Effective use of time, not more time or faster work, is the core idea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Refusing to delegate is a common time-management mistake, not the definition of managing time well.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Doing tasks quickly conflates speed with effectiveness; time management is about prioritisation, not simply working faster.

questions.learning_objective: State that time management means using available time more effectively, not eliminating leisure or refusing delegation.

questions.title: Time management prioritization principle
questions.question: Regarding time management, which of the followings is correct?

options.A: You need to decide what is really important and what can wait to effectively manage your time
options.B: Effective persons do everything for themselves and never delegate
options.C: Time management is an inborn skill that can't be acquired or improved
options.D: It is preferred to spend most of your time in the low value activities

explanations.A: Correct. Effective time management requires deciding what is really important and what can wait — a deliberate prioritization process, not an inborn trait or a habit of refusing delegation. This is the correctly-hedged statement among four options, three of which are false claims about time management. Prioritization is the mechanism that makes time management actionable day to day.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Effective people commonly delegate tasks rather than doing everything themselves; refusing to delegate is a common time-management failure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Time management is a learnable, improvable skill, not a fixed inborn trait.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Effective time management means minimising, not maximising, time spent on low-value activities.

questions.learning_objective: State that effective time management means deciding what is important versus what can wait.

questions.title: Definition of stress
questions.question: Which is correct about stress?

options.A: All people will respond exactly the same way to stress
options.B: Stress is the gap between our expectations and reality, it is a normal part of life
options.C: Stress is not affected by time management
options.D: There is only one source of stress

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stress responses vary considerably between individuals; there is no uniform response.
explanations.B: Correct. Stress is defined as the gap between our expectations and reality, and is described as a normal part of life. This definition explains why stress is both universal (everyone has expectations) and individually variable (everyone's reality and expectations differ), unlike the false-absolute claims in the other three options.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Time management is one of the factors that can widen or narrow the gap between expectations and reality, so stress is affected by it, not independent of it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stress has many possible sources (academic, personal, occupational, and more), not just one.

questions.learning_objective: State that stress is the gap between expectations and reality, and a normal part of life.

questions.title: Democratic leadership style
questions.question: In democratic leadership style, the leader:

options.A: Does not ask for a vote to get an important decision
options.B: Encourages others to volunteer for responsibilities and confirms commitments
options.C: Hogs all of the jobs and responsibilities
options.D: Uses silence and non-verbal expression rather than conversation and speaking

explanations.A: Incorrect. Withholding a vote on important decisions describes an autocratic, not democratic, style.
explanations.B: Correct. Democratic leadership style is defined by the leader encouraging others to volunteer for responsibilities and confirming their commitments — an actively participatory approach that seeks buy-in from the group. This active solicitation of votes/commitments is exactly what distinguishes democratic from autocratic leadership behaviours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hoarding all jobs and responsibilities describes an autocratic style, the opposite of democratic delegation and participation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Relying on silence and non-verbal cues instead of open discussion describes a laissez-faire or withdrawn style, not the actively participatory democratic style.

questions.learning_objective: Describe democratic leadership style as encouraging volunteering and confirming commitments.

questions.title: Justified breaches of confidentiality (exception)
questions.question: Conditions of justified breaches of confidentiality are all the followings EXCEPT:

options.B: For the public good in cases of infectious diseases like HIV
options.C: For present the physician's knowledge and skills
options.D: In courts of law as forensic experts

explanations.A: Not the exception. Patient consent is a genuine, recognised justification for breaching confidentiality, so it is not the answer to an EXCEPT question.
explanations.B: Not the exception. Public-good infectious-disease reporting (e.g. HIV) is a genuine, recognised justification, so it is not the answer either.
explanations.C: Correct. Presenting the physician's own knowledge and skills is NOT a justified condition for breaching confidentiality — disclosing patient information to showcase expertise serves the physician's own interest, not any recognised public-good or legal justification. This is the one option, among four, that does not belong to the genuine justified-breach list, making it the correct answer to an EXCEPT question.
explanations.D: Not the exception. Testimony in courts of law as a forensic expert is a genuine, recognised legal justification, so it is not the answer either.

questions.learning_objective: Identify "presenting the physician's own knowledge and skills" as not a justified condition for breaching confidentiality.
